answers.answer: In SCOPe, ferritins, ribonucleotide-reductase-like (RNR R2-like) proteins, and manganese catalases are all placed in class a (all-alpha), fold a.25 (ferritin-like: core of four helices, closed bundle, left-handed twist, one crossover connection), and the single superfamily a.25.1 (ferritin-like). Within that superfamily they sit in different families: a.25.1.1 Ferritin (ferritins, bacterioferritins, Dps/Dps-like proteins, rubrerythrin N-terminal domain), a.25.1.2 Ribonucleotide reductase-like (RNR R2 subunit, plus other diiron-carboxylate enzymes such as methane monooxygenase hydroxylase and stearoyl-ACP delta-9 desaturase), and a.25.1.3 Manganese catalase (e.g. Lactobacillus plantarum and Thermus thermophilus enzymes). The correct interpretation is therefore: (1) Superfamily level = probable common ancestry (homology). SCOP/SCOPe curators grouped them because they share not only the four-helix-bundle crossover topology but also a conserved dinuclear metal-binding site built from Glu and Glu-x-x-His motifs located at equivalent positions on the helices, which is treated as evidence of divergence from a common ancestral di-metal four-helix-bundle protein rather than convergence. (2) Family level = recognizable sequence/structure/function similarity. The three groups are separate families because they have low pairwise sequence identity and clearly different chemistries: ferritins use a di-iron ferroxidase site for Fe(II) oxidation and iron storage in a mineral core; RNR R2 uses a di-iron (or Mn/Fe) site to generate and stabilize a tyrosyl radical for nucleotide reduction (and relatives perform hydroxylation or desaturation); Mn catalases use a di-manganese site to disproportionate H2O2. (3) The different chemistries are an example of functional divergence after gene duplication: the ancestral scaffold and metal site were retained, while the metal preference (Fe vs Mn), redox partner, substrate access channels, second-shell residues, and oligomeric assembly (ferritin 24-mer shell, Dps 12-mer, Mn catalase hexamer, R2 dimer) diverged. Important limits: superfamily membership asserts homology, not function; it is unsafe to transfer EC number, substrate, metal identity, radical chemistry, or storage capacity from one family to another, and even within a.25.1.2 functions differ widely. Fold-level similarity (a.25) is even weaker evidence; other four-helix bundle folds such as a.24 (up-and-down bundle, e.g. hemerythrin, which also binds di-iron) are classified as separate folds, so helix-bundle resemblance alone must not be read as homology. For template-based modeling, cross-family a.25.1 templates can support the core bundle and the di-metal first-shell geometry, but not loops, termini, channels, quaternary structure, or ligand placement; models should use same-family templates where possible. Representative selection should be done per family (e.g. ASTRAL/SCOPe <40% identity subsets), since no single a.25.1 domain represents all three chemistries. Function assignment for an uncharacterized a.25.1 member requires external evidence: conserved motif analysis (ligand set and second-shell residues), metal content and EPR/spectroscopy, enzymatic assays, and genomic/phylogenetic context, in addition to the SCOPe placement. Finally, SCOPe's hierarchy here is inherited from manually curated SCOP 1.75; newer entries in SCOPe 2.0x are added mostly by automated matching to existing families, so novel ferritin-like chemistries may be placed by structural similarity rather than by functional evidence.
